course.title: Unity C# Scripting & Engine Architecture: From First Script to Optimized Game
course.description: A complete, hands-on journey through Unity's C# scripting system and engine architecture. Designed for developers who know C# basics but are new to Unity. Covers MonoBehaviour lifecycle, component patterns, input handling, physics, animation scripting, audio, UI scripting, and beginner optimization techniques. By the end, you will confidently write clean Unity C# code, understand how the engine executes your scripts, and build optimized game systems. Essential foundation for game developers, technical artists, and engine programmers.

blocks.value: How Unity Executes Your Code

Unity is not just a game editor. It is a runtime engine that executes your C# scripts frame by frame, 60 times per second (or more). Understanding this execution model is the foundation of everything you will build.

Unity uses a **component-based architecture**. Every object in your scene is a GameObject. GameObjects do nothing on their own. They become functional when you attach **Components** — scripts, renderers, colliders, audio sources, and more.
Your C# scripts are **Components**. They inherit from `MonoBehaviour`, which connects your code to the engine's lifecycle. The engine calls your methods automatically — you do not call them yourself.

blocks.alt: Diagram showing GameObject containing multiple Components: Transform, MeshRenderer, PlayerScript, Rigidbody, Collider
blocks.caption: A GameObject is a container of Components. Scripts are just one type of Component.

blocks.value: The Game Loop: Frame-by-Frame Execution
Games run in a loop: Process Input → Update Game State → Render Frame → Repeat. Unity handles this loop for you. Your scripts hook into specific points in this loop through **lifecycle methods**.
Key lifecycle methods you will use constantly:

items: `Awake()` — Called once when the script instance is loaded. Use for initialization that does not depend on other objects.
`OnEnable()` — Called when the object becomes active. Use for subscribing to events.
`Start()` — Called once before the first frame. Use for initialization that depends on other objects being ready.
`FixedUpdate()` — Called at a fixed timestep (default 50 times/second). Use for physics and rigidbody logic.
`Update()` — Called every frame. Use for input, movement, and gameplay logic.
`LateUpdate()` — Called after all Update() methods. Use for camera follow and post-update logic.
`OnDisable()` — Called when the object becomes inactive. Use for unsubscribing from events.
`OnDestroy()` — Called when the object is destroyed. Use for final cleanup.

blocks.output: Demonstrates the complete MonoBehaviour lifecycle with Debug.Log output for each phase.

blocks.value: Execution Order Matters

When multiple scripts exist, Unity calls their lifecycle methods in a specific order. By default, the order is undefined between scripts. This can cause bugs when Script A depends on Script B being initialized first.
Solutions for controlling execution order:

items: Use `Awake()` for self-initialization and `Start()` for cross-object initialization. All Awake() calls complete before any Start() calls.
Use `[DefaultExecutionOrder(100)]` attribute on a class to make it run earlier (lower numbers) or later (higher numbers).
Use `Script Execution Order` settings in Edit → Project Settings for fine-grained control.

blocks.output: Using DefaultExecutionOrder attribute to control script execution priority.

blocks.value: The Unity Editor vs Runtime
Unity has two distinct modes: **Edit Mode** (in the editor, not playing) and **Play Mode** (runtime, your game is running). Some APIs only work in one mode.
Key differences:

items: `[ExecuteInEditMode]` attribute makes a script run in the editor without pressing Play. Useful for editor tools and procedural generation previews.
`Application.isPlaying` checks if you are in Play Mode.
`#if UNITY_EDITOR` preprocessor directives compile code only in the editor build.
Editor scripts go in an `Editor` folder and cannot be included in builds.

blocks.output: Using ExecuteInEditMode and preprocessor directives for editor-only behavior.

blocks.question: You have two scripts: ScriptA needs to find ScriptB and call its method. Where should ScriptA find ScriptB?
blocks.explanation: Awake() is for self-initialization. All Awake() calls complete before any Start() calls. If ScriptA tries to find ScriptB in Awake(), ScriptB might not have initialized yet. Start() is the safe place for cross-object initialization because you are guaranteed all Awake() methods have finished. Update() would waste performance by searching every frame.

blocks.value: Creating and Attaching Scripts
In Unity, scripts are assets. You create them in the Project window, then attach them to GameObjects in the scene or prefabs.
Steps to create your first script:

items: Right-click in Project window → Create → C# Script → Name it 'PlayerMovement'
Double-click to open in Visual Studio or Rider
The script automatically inherits from MonoBehaviour
Drag the script onto a GameObject in the Hierarchy, or click Add Component → search for your script
The script is now a Component of that GameObject

blocks.output: Basic player movement script with serialized fields, component reference, input handling, and frame-rate independent movement.

blocks.value: The Inspector and Serialized Fields
Unity's Inspector shows public fields and `[SerializeField]` private fields. This is how you configure scripts without changing code.
Serialization rules:

items: Public fields are serialized by default (but this breaks encapsulation)
`[SerializeField]` on private fields keeps encapsulation while exposing to Inspector
`[HideInInspector]` hides a public field from the Inspector
`[Range(0, 100)]` adds a slider in the Inspector
`[Tooltip("Description here")]` shows hover text in the Inspector
`[Header("Group Name")]` creates labeled sections in the Inspector

blocks.output: Inspector-friendly script with headers, tooltips, range sliders, and organized sections.

blocks.value: Finding and Referencing Other Objects
Scripts rarely work alone. You need references to other GameObjects, components, and scripts. Unity provides multiple ways to find them.
Methods for finding objects:

items: `GetComponent<T>()` — Gets a component on the same GameObject
`GetComponentInChildren<T>()` — Searches children recursively
`GetComponentInParent<T>()` — Searches up the hierarchy
`FindObjectOfType<T>()` — Searches entire scene (slow, avoid in Update)
`GameObject.Find("Name")` — Finds by name (slow, fragile)
`GameObject.FindWithTag("Tag")` — Finds by tag (faster than by name)
`Transform.Find("Path")` — Finds child by path (e.g., 'Body/Hand/Weapon')
Serialized references — Drag in Inspector (fastest, most reliable)

blocks.output: Best practices for object references: serialized fields for reliability, caching FindObjectOfType in Start, and avoiding scene searches in Update.

blocks.value: The Transform: Position, Rotation, Scale
Every GameObject has a Transform component. It is the only component you cannot remove. It defines where the object is in 3D space.
Coordinate systems you must understand:

items: `transform.position` — World space (global coordinates, relative to scene origin)
`transform.localPosition` — Local space (relative to parent object's position)
`transform.rotation` — World space rotation as Quaternion
`transform.localRotation` — Local space rotation as Quaternion
`transform.eulerAngles` — World rotation in degrees (X, Y, Z)
`transform.localEulerAngles` — Local rotation in degrees
`transform.localScale` — Scale relative to parent

blocks.output: Transform manipulation: local vs world space, translation, rotation, LookAt, direction vectors, and smooth interpolation with Slerp.

blocks.question: Why is `[SerializeField] private float speed;` preferred over `public float speed;`?
options: It makes the variable faster at runtime
It keeps the field private (encapsulated) while still showing it in the Inspector
It automatically adds validation to the field
It prevents the field from being saved in the scene
blocks.correctAnswer: It keeps the field private (encapsulated) while still showing it in the Inspector
blocks.explanation: `public` fields break encapsulation — any script can modify them, leading to bugs. `[SerializeField] private` keeps the field encapsulated (only this class can modify it directly) while still exposing it to the Unity Inspector for designers to configure. This is a core principle of clean Unity architecture: expose configuration, hide implementation.

parts.partTitle: Part 3: Input Handling and Player Control

blocks.value: The Old Input System

Unity has two input systems. The **Old Input System** (built-in, default) uses `Input` class methods. The **New Input System** (package) uses actions and event-driven architecture. Beginners should understand both.
Old Input System key methods:

items: `Input.GetAxis("Horizontal")` — Returns -1 to 1 for WASD/arrow keys (smooth, interpolated)
`Input.GetAxisRaw("Horizontal")` — Returns -1, 0, or 1 (no smoothing, instant response)
`Input.GetKey(KeyCode.Space)` — True while key is held down
`Input.GetKeyDown(KeyCode.Space)` — True only on the frame the key is pressed
`Input.GetKeyUp(KeyCode.Space)` — True only on the frame the key is released
`Input.GetButton("Fire1")` — Uses Input Manager button mapping (cross-platform)
`Input.GetMouseButton(0)` — 0=left, 1=right, 2=middle click
`Input.mousePosition` — Screen coordinates in pixels (bottom-left origin)

blocks.output: Old Input System examples: GetAxis vs GetAxisRaw, GetKeyDown for single actions, GetKey for held actions, and mouse input.

blocks.value: The New Input System
The New Input System is event-driven and action-based. You define actions (like 'Move', 'Jump', 'Fire') and bind them to controls (keyboard, mouse, gamepad, touch).
Setup steps:

items: Install package: Window → Package Manager → Input System → Install
Create Input Actions asset: Right-click → Create → Input Actions
Define Action Maps (e.g., 'Player', 'UI', 'Vehicle')
Add Actions (e.g., 'Move', 'Jump') with bindings (WASD, arrow keys, gamepad stick)
Generate C# class from the asset for type-safe access

blocks.output: New Input System: action-based, event-driven input with proper subscription/unsubscription to prevent memory leaks.

blocks.value: Character Controller vs Rigidbody
Unity provides two main ways to move a player character. Each has distinct use cases and trade-offs.
**Character Controller** (script-based physics):

items: Does NOT use physics engine — you control movement exactly
Good for precise platformers, FPS games, and arcade-style movement
Handles slopes, steps, and collisions manually
`controller.Move()` takes a motion vector and handles collisions
Gravity and jumping must be coded manually

blocks.value: **Rigidbody** (physics engine):

items: Uses Unity's physics engine (PhysX)
Good for realistic physics, racing games, and physics puzzles
Forces, torque, and collisions are simulated automatically
`rb.AddForce()`, `rb.velocity`, `rb.MovePosition()`
Must use `FixedUpdate()` for physics code

blocks.output: Side-by-side comparison: CharacterController for precise FPS movement vs Rigidbody for physics-driven movement.

blocks.question: You are making a competitive FPS game where frame-perfect input response is critical. Which input method should you use for movement?
blocks.explanation: `GetAxis` applies smoothing and interpolation, which creates a slight delay between pressing a key and reaching full value. For competitive FPS games, this delay is unacceptable. `GetAxisRaw` returns exactly -1, 0, or 1 with no smoothing, giving instant, frame-perfect response. `GetKey` only checks one key, not the entire axis mapping. `mousePosition` is for cursor location, not movement input.

blocks.value: Unity's Physics Engine
Unity uses **NVIDIA PhysX** for 3D physics and **Box2D** for 2D physics. These are separate systems — 3D and 2D physics do not interact.
Core physics components:

items: `Rigidbody` — Makes an object respond to physics forces, gravity, and collisions
`Collider` — Defines the object's shape for collision detection (Box, Sphere, Capsule, Mesh)
`Rigidbody2D` — 2D physics equivalent with different properties
`Collider2D` — 2D collision shapes (Box, Circle, Polygon, Edge)
`PhysicsMaterial` — Controls friction and bounciness

blocks.value: Critical rule: Never modify `transform.position` on a GameObject with a Rigidbody. This teleports the object and breaks physics consistency. Use `rb.MovePosition()` or forces instead.

blocks.output: Rigidbody configuration and proper physics manipulation in FixedUpdate.

blocks.value: Collision Detection Methods
Unity provides three ways to detect collisions. Choose based on your needs.
**1. Collision Messages** (physical contact between Colliders):

items: `OnCollisionEnter(Collision collision)` — Called when colliders first touch
`OnCollisionStay(Collision collision)` — Called every frame while touching
`OnCollisionExit(Collision collision)` — Called when colliders separate
Requires at least one Rigidbody on either object
Provides `Collision` data: contact points, impulse, relative velocity

blocks.value: **2. Trigger Messages** (non-physical overlap detection):

items: `OnTriggerEnter(Collider other)` — Called when entering a trigger volume
`OnTriggerStay(Collider other)` — Called every frame while inside
`OnTriggerExit(Collider other)` — Called when leaving
Enable 'Is Trigger' on a Collider to make it a trigger
Triggers detect overlap but do not physically block movement

blocks.value: **3. Physics Queries** (manual checks without collision):

items: `Physics.Raycast()` — Shoot a line and check what it hits
`Physics.SphereCast()` — Like raycast but with thickness
`Physics.OverlapSphere()` — Find all colliders in a sphere
`Physics.BoxCast()` — Cast a box shape
`Physics.SphereOverlap()` — Find colliders overlapping a sphere

blocks.output: Complete physics examples: collision handling, trigger zones, raycasting for interaction, ground checks, and explosion damage with OverlapSphere.

blocks.value: Layer Masks and Physics Filtering
Layer Masks control which objects physics queries and collisions affect. They are essential for performance and correct behavior.
How layer masks work:

items: Assign layers in the Inspector top-right dropdown (Default, Enemy, Ground, UI, etc.)
`LayerMask.GetMask("Enemy", "Obstacle")` creates a mask for multiple layers
`1 << LayerMask.NameToLayer("Enemy")` creates a mask for one layer using bit shifting
Pass the mask to Raycast, OverlapSphere, etc. to filter results
Use Physics.IgnoreLayerCollision(layer1, layer2) to prevent specific layers from colliding

blocks.output: Layer mask creation, combination with bitwise OR, filtering physics queries, and ignoring layer collisions.

blocks.question: You need to detect when a player enters a pickup zone but the pickup should not physically block the player. What should you use?
options: OnTriggerEnter with 'Is Trigger' enabled on the pickup's collider
Physics.Raycast from the player every frame
blocks.correctAnswer: OnTriggerEnter with 'Is Trigger' enabled on the pickup's collider
blocks.explanation: Triggers detect overlap without physical response — perfect for pickups, checkpoints, and zones. Enable 'Is Trigger' on the Collider component. `OnCollisionEnter` requires physical collision and would block movement. `Physics.Raycast` only checks a line, not a volume. `Vector3.Distance` works but is inefficient for many pickups and does not handle complex shapes.

parts.partTitle: Part 5: Animation Scripting and State Machines

blocks.value: The Animator Component
Unity's animation system uses the **Animator component** with an **Animator Controller** asset. The controller is a state machine that manages animation clips and transitions.
Key concepts:

items: **Animator Controller** — State machine asset that defines states, transitions, and parameters
**Animation States** — Individual animation clips (Idle, Walk, Run, Attack)
**Transitions** — Rules for moving between states (based on parameters, exit time, or conditions)
**Parameters** — Variables controlled by scripts: Float, Int, Bool, Trigger
**Layers** — Multiple animation layers for upper body, lower body, full body
**Avatar Masks** — Restrict animation to specific body parts

blocks.output: Animator parameter control with hashed lookups for performance, trigger handling, and animation events.

blocks.value: Animation Events
Animation Events let you call methods at specific frames of an animation. This is how you synchronize gameplay logic with visual feedback.
Common use cases:

items: Deal damage on the exact frame a punch connects
Spawn footstep particle/sound when foot touches ground
Enable/disable hitbox colliders during attack animations
Spawn projectile when gun recoil animation peaks
Trigger camera shake on heavy attack impact

blocks.output: Animation Events for combat timing: enabling hitboxes, playing effects, spawning objects, and parameterized events.

blocks.value: Blend Trees and 2D Animation
**Blend Trees** smoothly blend between multiple animations based on parameters. They are essential for natural movement.
Types of blend trees:

items: **1D Blend Tree** — Blends based on a single float (e.g., Speed: Idle → Walk → Run)
**2D Blend Tree** — Blends based on two floats (e.g., Velocity X and Z for 8-directional movement)
**2D Simple Directional** — For distinct directions (up, down, left, right)
**2D Freeform Cartesian** — For continuous 2D space (top-down movement)

blocks.output: 2D blend tree for 8-directional movement and 2D sprite animation with direction handling and sprite flipping.

blocks.question: Why should you use `Animator.StringToHash()` instead of passing strings directly to `animator.SetBool()`?
options: It makes the code more readable
It avoids string allocation and dictionary lookup every frame, improving performance
It is required for the Animator to work
blocks.correctAnswer: It avoids string allocation and dictionary lookup every frame, improving performance
blocks.explanation: Every time you pass a string like `animator.SetBool("IsWalking", true)`, Unity must hash that string to find the parameter internally. This allocates memory and performs a dictionary lookup. By caching `Animator.StringToHash("IsWalking")` in Awake(), you precompute the hash and pass an integer ID instead. This is a zero-allocation, O(1) lookup — critical when called every frame in Update().

parts.partTitle: Part 6: Audio, UI, and Scene Management

blocks.value: Audio System
Unity's audio uses the **AudioSource** component to play sounds and the **AudioListener** component (usually on the Main Camera) to hear them.
Audio best practices:

items: Use **Audio Mixer** groups (SFX, Music, Voice) for volume control and effects
Pool AudioSources for frequent sounds (gunshots, footsteps) instead of creating/destroying
Use `AudioSource.PlayOneShot()` for overlapping sounds on the same source
Use `AudioSource.PlayClipAtPoint()` for 3D positioned sounds that auto-cleanup
Compress audio assets appropriately: Vorbis for music, ADPCM for short SFX

blocks.output: Complete AudioManager with singleton pattern, mixer groups, sound pooling, random pitch variation, 3D positioned audio, volume control in decibels, and music fading.

blocks.value: Unity UI (uGUI) Scripting
Unity's UI system (uGUI) uses **Canvas** as the root, **RectTransform** for positioning, and various UI components (Text, Image, Button, Slider, etc.).
Canvas render modes:

items: **Screen Space - Overlay** — UI renders on top of everything, always visible
**Screen Space - Camera** — UI rendered by a specific camera, can be affected by camera effects
**World Space** — UI exists in 3D world (in-world screens, holograms, health bars above enemies)

blocks.output: Complete UIManager with event-driven HUD updates, damage flash, animated score, world-space damage numbers, pause menu with time scaling, and button click handlers.

blocks.value: Scene Management and Loading
Unity uses **Scenes** to organize content. You load scenes to switch between menus, levels, and game states.
Loading methods:

items: `SceneManager.LoadScene(index)` — Instant load, causes frame hitch
`SceneManager.LoadSceneAsync(name)` — Loads in background without freezing
`Additive` loading — Loads scene on top of current (good for UI overlays, streaming open worlds)
`LoadSceneMode.Single` — Replaces current scene (default)
Always use `Async` for gameplay to avoid freezing the player

blocks.output: Async scene loading with progress bar, additive scene loading for overlays, and platform-aware quit handling.

blocks.value: Persistent Data: PlayerPrefs and ScriptableObjects
Games need to save settings, progress, and high scores. Unity provides two built-in solutions.
**PlayerPrefs** — Simple key-value storage (not secure, limited to basic types):

items: Stores int, float, string only
Saved automatically to disk
Easy to hack — do NOT store sensitive data (passwords, purchase status)
Good for: volume settings, graphics quality, last played level, username

blocks.value: **ScriptableObjects** — Data assets that live in the project, not in scenes:

items: Create data containers that designers can configure
Shared across scenes without duplication
Cannot be modified at runtime in builds (read-only)
Good for: weapon stats, enemy configurations, game balance data

blocks.output: Type-safe PlayerPrefs wrapper for settings persistence, and ScriptableObject data containers for designer-configurable weapon stats.

blocks.question: You need to load a large open-world level without freezing the game for several seconds. Which approach should you use?
options: Instantiate all terrain chunks manually in a coroutine
Use SceneManager.LoadSceneAdditive("OpenWorld") on top of the menu scene
blocks.explanation: `LoadScene()` freezes the entire game until loading completes — unacceptable for large levels. `LoadSceneAsync()` loads in the background while your game continues running, allowing you to show a progress bar and keep the player engaged. Manual instantiation is complex and error-prone. Additive loading keeps the menu scene active, which is not what you want when transitioning to gameplay.
